# What's in MICS6 data? {#c02-whats-in-data}

MICS is a household survey, not a school assessment and not one flat file. It contains several questionnaires and data files with different units of observation.

Many errors in MICS analysis happen before a statistical model is run. Using the wrong file, misunderstanding who appears in the `fs` dataset, merging on an incomplete identifier, or treating a reading skip as ordinary missing data can all change the population represented in an analysis.

The [UNICEF MICS6 Manual for Statistical Data Analysis](https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/MICS6-manual-for-stats-data-analysis-English_2020_v2.pdf) is the main reference for the MICS6 questionnaire structure and standard indicator construction. The [UNICEF Foundational Learning Skills Module resource](https://data.unicef.org/resources/the-foundational-learning-skills-module/) provides additional background on the learning assessment.

A useful way to think about MICS is as a set of linked datasets:

```text
HOUSEHOLD
   │
   ├── household characteristics
   │
   ├── household member 1
   ├── household member 2
   ├── household member 3
   │        │
   │        ├── may have an individual questionnaire
   │        │
   │        └── may be selected for the 5–17 questionnaire
   │
   └── household member n
```

The household questionnaire tells us about the household and everyone listed in it. Additional questionnaires collect more detailed information for particular populations, including women, men, children under five and one randomly selected child aged 5–17 per household.

For foundational-learning research, the most important files are usually `fs` (the selected child aged 5–17), `hl` (all household members) and `hh` (the household). Researchers may also need other files for particular questions.

[Files, units of observation and identifiers](#c02-files) explains these files and their identifiers.
